---
title: "What are the lift and drag polars from −15° to +15° angle of attack?"
---


::: {#702297ee .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
alpha = np.linspace(-15, 15, 121)
p = polars(alpha, V=6.0)

a_stall, _ = stall(6.0)
```
:::


**Answer.** @fig-polars. Lift is linear to about
[10\.3°]{.key} and drag rises steeply either side of zero,
so the useful range is narrow. These are the section's curves at one fixed
speed, not the aircraft's performance — the glider trims nose-higher and slower
than the polar's best point, which is why the glide entry solves for trim
instead of reading a figure off here.

::: {.callout-note}
## Assumed
1. **Fixed 6 m/s** — matches chapter 1's BFG run.
:::

::: {#cell-fig-polars .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.0))

ax[0].plot(alpha, p["CL"])
ax[0].set_xlabel(r"$\alpha$ [deg]"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$C_L$")
ax[0].set_title("Lift curve")

ax[1].plot(alpha, p["CD"])
ax[1].set_xlabel(r"$\alpha$ [deg]"); ax[1].set_ylabel(r"$C_D$")
ax[1].set_title("Drag curve")

ax[2].plot(p["CD"], p["CL"])
ax[2].set_xlabel(r"$C_D$"); ax[2].set_ylabel(r"$C_L$")
ax[2].set_title("Drag polar")

# Where the glider actually flies, on the two curves that are read against alpha.
for a in ax[:2]:
    a.axvspan(0, a_stall, color="0.92", zorder=0)
for a in ax:
    a.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
